title: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: Between the Gothic crossing of the Danube in 376 and the deposition of the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna in 476, the western half of the Roman Empire lost its provinces, its capital city's security and finally its emperors, while the eastern half survived.
card: A century of crises broke Roman rule in the West: Goths fleeing the Huns destroyed an imperial army at Adrianople in 378, Rome itself was sacked in 410 and 455, and the Vandals took the rich African provinces. In 476 the officer Odoacer killed the general Orestes, deposed his young son Romulus Augustulus and ruled Italy as a king. Historians still argue whether this was a catastrophic collapse or a slower transformation, and whether 476 is the right end date at all.
what:
The fall of the Western Roman Empire is the name given to the loss of imperial government in the Latin-speaking western provinces during the late fourth and fifth centuries CE. In 376, Gothic Tervingi under Fritigern and Alavivus, displaced by the Huns, asked the eastern emperor Valens for admission and were ferried across the lower Danube. Starved and exploited by the Roman commanders Lupicinus and Maximus, they revolted near Marcianopolis, and on 9 August 378 (Julian) they destroyed Valens' army near Adrianople; the emperor was killed and, by Ammianus Marcellinus' account, barely a third of his force escaped.

After Theodosius I died in 395 the empire was governed as eastern and western halves. The western court withdrew from Milan to Ravenna in 402; Vandals, Alans, Suevi and Burgundians crossed the Rhine at the end of 406; Britain slipped out of imperial control; and in 410 Alaric's Goths entered Rome through the Salarian Gate and plundered it. By 439 the Vandals held Carthage and nearly all of Roman North Africa. In 455, after the murders of Valentinian III and Petronius Maximus, the Vandal king Gaiseric sacked Rome for about two weeks and carried the empress Eudoxia and her daughters to Carthage.

In 475 the general Orestes drove the emperor Julius Nepos to Dalmatia and raised his own son Romulus, nicknamed Augustulus. In August 476 troops in Italy proclaimed Odoacer king; he killed Orestes near Placentia, killed Orestes' brother Paulus at Ravenna, and on or soon after 4 September deposed Romulus, sparing him with a pension and sending him to Campania. The imperial regalia went to Zeno in Constantinople, and the eastern empire continued. Writers of the sixth century such as Marcellinus Comes and Jordanes treated 476 as the end of the western empire. Modern historians disagree about whether the process was a violent collapse or a gradual transformation, and some argue that Nepos, who lived until 480, was the last legitimate western emperor.

uncertainty.note: Start = the Gothic crossing of the Danube (376). End = the deposition of Romulus Augustulus, dated by Mathisen to on or soon after 4 September 476 (Julian), i.e. 5 September 476 proleptic Gregorian; Paulus was killed on 31 August or 4 September, so the exact day is not fixed. Mathisen argues the western line properly ends with the death of Julius Nepos in 480, hence end_plus_years 4. The choice of start date is a convention: Heather dates the final collapse of imperial structures to 468–476.

how: Causes and sequence. (1) External pressure: the Huns' arrival north of the Black Sea in 375 drove Gothic groups to seek refuge in Roman territory, and in 376 Valens allowed the Tervingi across the Danube. Supply failure and the greed of the commanders Lupicinus and Maximus turned refugees into rebels by 377. (2) Military shock: at Adrianople on 9 August 378 Valens attacked before his nephew Gratian's western army arrived; Gothic cavalry routed the Roman horse, the crowded infantry broke in the afternoon heat, and Valens died. A modern estimate cited by Lenski puts Roman dead near 26,000 of about 40,000. (3) Political division and weak centre: after 395 the halves were ruled separately; the western court sat at Ravenna from 402, generals such as Stilicho and Aetius dominated emperors, and both were murdered (408 and 454). (4) Loss of territory and taxes: the Rhine crossing of 406, the loss of Britain, the sack of Rome in 410 and the Vandal conquest of North Africa by 439 removed provinces whose agricultural taxes paid the army; Heather describes a downward spiral in which lost land meant lost revenue and fewer troops. (5) Endgame: after 455 western emperors were made and unmade by army commanders. Orestes raised his son in 475; on 23 August 476 the troops in Italy proclaimed Odoacer, an officer of Scirian and Hunnic background by one account, as their king. Odoacer killed Orestes and Paulus, deposed Romulus, sent the regalia east and governed Italy as a king while the eastern emperor remained the nominal sovereign. Explanations differ: Gibbon stressed internal decay, Heather external pressure, Ward-Perkins violent invasion and chance, and the 'transformation' school continuity.
why_it_matters: The deposition of 476 ended the line of emperors resident in the western Mediterranean, and Jordanes, writing in 551, already treated it as the moment from which Gothic kings held Rome and Italy. Odoacer ruled Italy as a king for about thirteen years until Theodoric's Ostrogoths replaced him in 493, and across the former western provinces landowners had to adapt to local Germanic kings backed by armed followings, the political frame of early medieval western Europe. The consequences went beyond politics. Heather argues that when the imperial bureaucracy disappeared, so did the careers that had sustained elite literacy, and that without powerful western emperors the later papacy as a monarchy is hard to imagine. Ward-Perkins points to a sharp fall in material comfort and in everyday reading and writing across the West. Meanwhile the eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, survived, so Roman imperial government carried on in the eastern Mediterranean under Zeno and his successors. The fall also shaped how later centuries thought about empires: Gibbon read it as a lesson in the decay that follows overextension, and modern historians remain split between those who stress collapse and those who stress transformation. Counterfactuals are built into that debate: Heather and Ward-Perkins both stress chance events such as the arrival of the Huns, so had the Huns not pushed the Goths across the Danube in 376 the western empire might have lasted far longer, and Ward-Perkins argues that the East survived largely because a strait of sea shielded its richest provinces, something the West did not have.

August 410: Alaric's Goths enter Rome through the Salarian Gate, burn houses near it and plunder the city.

beats.action: region.fill { region: 'Roman North Africa', to_polity: 'Vandals', anchor: [36.853056, 10.323056] }
beats.caption: By 439 the Vandals hold Carthage and nearly all Roman North Africa, cutting the western government off from some of its richest tax-paying land.
451: a Roman and Visigothic army under Aetius and Theodorid halts Attila's Huns in Gaul.
455: Valentinian III and then Petronius Maximus are murdered. Gaiseric's Vandals sack Rome for about two weeks and carry the empress and princesses to Carthage.
August 476: soldiers in Italy proclaim Odoacer king. He catches and kills the patrician Orestes near Placentia.
September 476: Odoacer enters Ravenna and deposes the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, sparing him with an income of 6,000 gold coins and exile in Campania.

beats.caption: No emperor now resides in the West. Kings rule Italy, the regalia go to Zeno in Constantinople, and the eastern empire carries on.
480: Julius Nepos, whom some historians count as the last lawful western emperor, is killed in Dalmatia.

perspectives.holder: Edward Gibbon, The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, ch. 38 ('General Observations')
perspectives.account: The fall was the natural result of overextension: prosperity bred decay, the division of the empire weakened the West, reliance on barbarian troops corrupted discipline, and Christianity drew energy and wealth away from civic and military life.

perspectives.holder: The 'transformation' school associated with Peter Brown (the 'Reformers' in O'Donnell's terms)
perspectives.account: Late antiquity should be read as a long transformation rather than an end, with weight on continuity, the surviving East, and religious and cultural change; O'Donnell counts himself among this group.

perspectives.holder: Peter Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire: A New History (2005)
perspectives.account: Internal decline does not explain the fifth-century collapse; Hunnic pressure pushed larger, more unified Germanic groups into the empire, and lost territory meant lost taxes and armies in a spiral that ended imperial structures in the West between 468 and 476.

perspectives.holder: Bryan Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005)
perspectives.account: The end of Roman rule was violent and painful, and archaeology shows a steep fall in material comfort and literacy; 476 itself matters little because the last western emperors had already lost real power, and the East survived mainly through the shelter of its geography.

perspectives.holder: Ralph W. Mathisen (De Imperatoribus Romanis) versus Geoffrey S. Nathan and most scholars
perspectives.account: Mathisen argues that Julius Nepos, recognised in the East and still minting coins in Odoacer's Italy, was the last legitimate western emperor until his death in 480; Nathan notes that most scholars take Romulus' deposition in 476 as the end of the western empire as a political entity.

numbers.label: Roman dead at Adrianople, 378 (modern estimate)
numbers.note: Single modern estimate (Hoffmann, cited by Lenski) of about 26,000 dead from an army of about 40,000; Lenski's text says two-thirds of the eastern army died, and Ammianus says barely a third escaped. No independent range was found.

numbers.label: Length of the Vandal sack of Rome, 455
numbers.note: Fourteen days per Victor of Tonnena as reported by Mathisen; Procopius gives no duration. Entry date is 24 May 455 (Julian) in Mathisen; other modern accounts put it in early June.

numbers.label: Income granted to the deposed Romulus Augustulus
numbers.note: Figure stated in the Anonymus Valesianus (2.38) and repeated by Mathisen and Nathan; Nathan likens it to a wealthy senator's income.

numbers.label: Duration of the western empire by Jordanes' reckoning
numbers.note: Jordanes' own count from Augustus to Augustulus; a sixth-century reckoning, not a modern measurement.

audience_note: Describes war, sieges and the plunder of cities, and starving refugees forced to give up their own people, including children of their leaders, as slaves in exchange for dogs to eat; no graphic imagery.

importance.justification: The end of Roman imperial government in the West is a standard turning point in world history between antiquity and the Middle Ages and reshaped the political map of Europe and the Mediterranean, so it must be visible at whole-planet view.
